script.title: A Satellite Has Watched the Sun Nonstop Since 2010
script.description: The Solar Dynamics Observatory captures high-resolution imagery of the Sun's dynamic surface and corona every twelve seconds. This narration explores the magnetic loops, massive flares, and extreme temperature mysteries of our central star.

shots.narration: Since 2010, the Solar Dynamics Observatory has imaged the Sun every twelve seconds, sending back 1.5 terabytes daily.
The spacecraft captures dynamic flares and active regions across multiple wavelengths of light.
The Sun measures 1.39 million kilometres across, a distance where 109 Earths could fit side by side.
Its surface reaches 5,500 °C, yet its thin outer atmosphere, the corona, rises above a million degrees.
Glowing plasma traces magnetic field lines, forming loops that can each be larger than many Earths.
A large solar flare releases as much energy as millions of hydrogen bombs exploding at once.
Flare light reaches Earth in eight minutes twenty seconds, while particle clouds take one to three days.
Roughly every eleven years, the Sun's magnetic poles swap places as plasma arches across its limb.
